```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.align = "center")
```

## The idea

A maze is a spanning tree of a grid. Every cell is a vertex, every pair of
orthogonally adjacent cells is a candidate edge, and carving a passage means
keeping that edge. `generate_maze()` offers five classic ways to build such a
tree, chosen with `algorithm`. They all produce a *perfect* maze -- connected
and acyclic -- but each leaves a recognisable texture.

Start by creating a small reproducible maze with the default algorithm:

```{r create}
library(mazegenerator)

maze <- generate_maze(8, 12, start = c(1, 1), seed = 42)
maze
```

## Randomized depth-first search

The default, `algorithm = "dfs"`, is often called the *recursive backtracker*.
Despite the name, this implementation is iterative: a list is used as a stack,
so it does not depend on R's recursion limit.

At each step, the generator:

1. finds the orthogonal neighbors of the current cell;
2. randomly chooses one that has not been visited;
3. carves a passage and pushes that cell onto the stack;
4. returns to the previous cell when it reaches a dead end.

The process ends after every cell has been visited. Because the walk commits to
a direction until it runs out of room, DFS produces long, winding corridors and
comparatively few dead ends.

```{r plot, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
plot_maze(maze)
```

DFS is the only algorithm that produces a single contiguous walk, so it is the
only one that records `traversal` and `visitation_order`. Those two fields are
`NULL` for every other algorithm, and `plot_maze(show_path = TRUE)` is therefore
available only for DFS mazes.

## The other four algorithms

```{r algorithms, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
for (algo in c("prim", "kruskal", "wilson", "eller")) {
  plot_maze(
    generate_maze(8, 12, seed = 42, algorithm = algo),
    main = algo
  )
}
```

- **`"prim"`** grows one tree outward from `start`, repeatedly carving a
  uniformly random wall on the frontier between the tree and the rest of the
  grid. The result branches evenly and is full of short dead ends -- visually
  the opposite of DFS.
- **`"kruskal"`** shuffles every internal wall and carves each one whose two
  sides still belong to different components, tracked with a union-find. It has
  no bias toward `start` at all, since it never looks at where the maze began.
- **`"wilson"`** builds a *uniform* spanning tree using loop-erased random
  walks: every perfect maze on the grid is equally likely. That statistical
  purity costs time, because the early walks wander a long way before they
  find the tree.
- **`"eller"`** sweeps one row at a time, merging cells into sets and carrying
  only a single row of state. It is the algorithm to reach for when the grid is
  too tall to hold in memory at once.

## Why the result is a perfect maze

Each algorithm reaches the same invariant by a different argument, but the
outcome is identical: no carved passage ever joins two cells that were already
connected, and carving continues until everything is connected. A connected
graph without cycles is a tree, so there is exactly one simple route between
any pair of cells.

For a maze with *rows × columns* cells, the generator creates exactly one fewer
unique passage than the number of cells.

```{r properties}
length(maze$passages)
maze$rows * maze$cols - 1
```

Every maze also records `carve_order`, the passages in the order they were
opened. That is what `animate_maze()` replays, and it is defined for all five
algorithms -- watching Prim spread outward next to Wilson's disconnected
fragments snapping together is the clearest way to see the difference.

## Adding loops

`open_walls` breaks the invariant on purpose. After generation, each remaining
internal wall is independently removed with the given probability, *braiding*
the maze:

```{r braided}
braided <- generate_maze(8, 12, seed = 42, open_walls = 0.3)
braided
```

A braided maze is no longer a tree, so routes are no longer unique -- which is
exactly what makes it interesting to search.

## Finding a route

`solve_maze()` searches the passage graph, with `algorithm` choosing between
three classic strategies:

- **`"astar"`** (the default) is goal-directed. Manhattan distance is an
  admissible heuristic because maze movement is orthogonal and every step costs
  the same, so the path it returns is guaranteed shortest.
- **`"dijkstra"`** is the same search with the heuristic dropped: it expands
  uniformly outward from `start`, ignoring where `end` is.
- **`"bfs"`** is the unweighted special case, a plain FIFO queue. It expands in
  rings of equal distance, and requires every step to cost the same.

```{r solve, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
solution <- solve_maze(maze)
head(solution)
plot_maze(maze, solution = solution)
```

All three return a shortest route; what differs is how much of the maze they
touch getting there. `trace = TRUE` records every expansion, which is both what
`animate_solution()` replays and an easy way to count the work:

```{r expansions}
big <- generate_maze(40, 40, seed = 123, algorithm = "kruskal")

vapply(c("astar", "dijkstra", "bfs"), function(algo) {
  traced <- solve_maze(big, algorithm = algo, trace = TRUE)
  length(attr(traced, "search_trace")$steps)
}, integer(1))
```

The heuristic is what separates A-star from the other two. Note that the gap
depends entirely on how far apart `start` and `end` are: for `algorithm = "dfs"`
the end cell is the last cell the walk visited, which frequently lands close to
the start, and then all three algorithms do nearly the same work. The other four
algorithms instead place `end` at the cell furthest from `start`, which is why
the comparison above uses one of them.

`solve_maze()` also accepts a matrix in which selected values represent walkable
cells. When diagonal movement is enabled, Euclidean distance and diagonal step
costs are used so the search still returns a shortest path -- and because those
steps no longer cost the same, `"bfs"` rejects that combination.
